speechtext:
Thank you very much. I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) for raising this problem and going to the trouble of presenting a bill and bringing in a very well documented case for our consideration.
I was very much interested in some of the things he said and in his knowledge of the situation with regard to first world war veterans. I took particular note of the indication he gave that he realizes that men who served in an actual theatre of war in the first world war were not at times too kindly disposed to those who did not reach that theatre of war.
Even in a theatre of war such as Belgium and France, the men who were up in the front lines were not too enthusiastic about people who were serving in the base installations. At times that attitude of mind prevailed even with regard to those men who were at rear headquarters and battalion headquarters just behind the lines. That attitude of mind prevailed for a long time, and I am sure it affected the drawing up of legislation in this house and the definition of the word "veteran." The word veteran, to a man who fought in the first world war, meant a person who had actually served in a theatre of war and who had been in grave danger.
The second world war changed the picture very considerably, because men and women from Canada served virtually all over the world, and places in the first world war which
War Veterans Allowance Act were free from serious attack became theatres of war in the second world war. A man who served in Britain in the second world war served in a theatre of war, whereas in the first world war this was not the case; he had to cross the channel before he really ran into any danger. Those of us who were in Britain in the second world war know perfectly well that we were often in a much safer place in a military camp than were civilians in the towns and cities.
So the word "veteran" has changed its meaning over the years and is not as distinctive as it was just subsequent to the first world war. This has caused some difficulty in the Department of Veterans Affairs when legislation was being drawn up, as well as to the veterans organizations. The definition of the word "veteran" has been considerably modified, as is instanced in the notes to the bill in front of us. I quote from the reference to section 30, subsection 3, where a veteran is described as a person who served in the United Kingdom during the first world war for at least 365 days prior to November 12, 1918. Enlargement of the term "veteran" has caused some heartburning in official circles for a long time.
The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. McIntosh) indicated the interest of people now in the older veterans, and the advantages of the War Veterans Allowance Act. Of course, it was originally drawn up, as he said, to make provision for men who served in a theatre of war-men who served in the trenches and returned without any visible sign of having served overseas-that is, they were not wounded. Yet as time elapsed medical officers observed that a number of the men who had served in the trenches aged prematurely; unwounded men who had perhaps served for a year or two years or even longer during the engagements in France came home to Canada without any extra provision being made for them at all. But the aging factor became apparent and, consequently, the War Veterans Allowance Act was developed and veterans aged 60 and over, in difficult economic circumstances, became eligible for assistance under that measure.
With the development of social security and a changing attitude in Canada, the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act have been extended, and I think properly so. The proposal now placed before us is one which is worthy of very serious consideration. I recall, when I was minister of veterans affairs, dealing with this particular problem of the

War Veterans Allowance Act number of days of service in the United Kingdom. The question of the cut-off date arose. As time goes on, people say: That should be shifted. I think it is only right that it should be shifted with changing conditions. I well recall that we took a good look at the survivors of the South African war. I remember saying to my officials: The survivors of that war are in their eighties and nineties; let us relax the regulations as far as they are concerned, and at least give them a few years of happiness if we can provide some assistance for them. And we did. We were able to assist some of them. Yet under the terms of the act as it stood, they did not qualify.
Now we have reached the stage where the average age of those who served in the first world war is 71. These men are a vanishing race. Some of them, who volunteered for service and who, through no fault of their own, did not reach the theatre of war in France, or who, again through no fault of their own, were in Britain for fewer than 365 days, perhaps require a little more attention than has been given to them up to the present time.
I am not sure that the bill as presently drafted may not need some modification. It is perhaps the type of bill the subject matter of which should be referred to the committee on veterans affairs. Unless this is done it will lapse and this particular problem will not receive the attention it deserves. It will not receive the attention it deserves because the spokesman for the government, the hon. member for Chambly-Rouville (Mr. Pilon) raised the usual objections which come from officials. He said it would be difficult for the department to administer; that it would be hard to determine the number of people who might qualify.
Well, all these difficulties can be overcome. The records are there; they just have to be searched. They show when a man enlisted, how long he was in Canada and how long he was overseas. They have been carefully kept and this is not an insuperable job at all. I was amused to hear the objections which emanate from officialdom. I do not mind the officials raising the objections; that is their job. They have to point out to ministers and parliamentary secretaries the difficulties in the way of new legislation, and they are responsible for showing that these difficulties exist. But as far as the government is concerned, it should deal with these difficulties and take the necessary steps to put some new measure into effect, if it is found as a matter of policy to be worth while.

I think that a bill of this nature is commendable and that the subject matter should be carefully studied. A spokesman for the government might have undertaken to do this. The parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Carter) is present, and, given the chance, he might have said earlier that his department intended to consider this question and, perhaps, bring in some amendments later in the year. If on the other hand the department intends to do nothing, then the subject matter should be referred to the standing committee on veterans affairs. Let them have a go at it. Officials could be called in to indicate the problems which arise and others could, perhaps, show how these problems could be overcome.
I was glad to hear the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) indicate their approval in principle of this measure. They paid their respects to those who have served abroad, and I think Canada generally has been appreciative of those who have volunteered to serve abroad in the defence of freedom. If they are older people, now, I think it is within the capability of the committee to say whether something might not be done for them.
I raise just one question before I sit down. I wonder whether it would be advisable to make a strictly proportionate estimate of the amount of money which might be paid. Perhaps an easier rule of thumb could be introduced in this regard, because you might get 201 over 365 for one man and 59 over 365 for another. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it might be simplified by being divided into three parts, or something of that nature. Even that eventually would not satisfy everyone, but it would remove part of the difficulty of having to deal with, say, 500 people each one having a different percentage of entitlement. However, that is something the committee could decide. I would like to express my approval of the bill, and if it comes to a vote I shall certainly vote in favour of it.

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at five o'clock I was saying that a great many Canadians who want to see Canada free at last from any colonial signs also want Canada to be recognized as a sovereign, independent and free nation.
If so, why did the Prime Minister, after indicating a clear track in Winnipeg, suddenly resort to a switch if not to please some fanatics still existing in our country, not only on one side but on both sides, because I have always considered that those who wanted to see Canada connected with foreign affairs as well as those who do not want to see anything but their own personal interest, are hindering national unity.
Throughout Canada, the press was critical of the government's action. I should like to quote an editorial which was published in Le Devoir and which was written by one of French Canada's most moderate newspapermen, a man who has no hallucinations, Mr. Paul Sauriol. This is what he had to say:
Dividing the resolution would make it possible for the government to get out of a mess. A resolution on a distinctive flag and on the anthem O Canada would surely be carried.
Here, I must congratulate Your Honour for the decision you took yesterday with respect to the resolution. Perhaps it would not have compromised national unity in the long run, because personally I do not feel that the flag issue can strengthen national unity in Canada. There are other factors which will help to strengthen Canadian unity and not just the adoption of a flag or a national anthem. But separate resolutions will help us to consider the matter objectively.
As for the resolution on the union jack and God Save the Queen, they are not essential to the election promise concerning those British symbols. In any case, separate resolutions would help to indicate the subordination of the old symbols to the new ones.

Mr. Sauriol concluded his editorial of June 2 by saying:
The union jack and God Save the Queen are not in England symbols restricted to the crown as such; they are the national flag and the national anthem of the United Kingdom. Mr. Pearson's proposals emphasize the British character of the crown in Canada. These traces of imperialism are bound to create deep uneasiness in the province of Quebec at the present time.
Not only in Quebec, but also in many other Canadian provinces.
At this point, I would like to say that we Quebeckers would object just as much to a symbol representing France which is, in the final analysis, the country where we have our roots, whose soil has nurtured our own French Canadian roots-our forefathers came from France-but we would not accept a French symbol as an emblem for Canada. We want to be what we have always been, true Canadians who are determined to remain so, Canadians who want emblems and symbols meant especially for them and for nobody else in the whole wide world.
Then again, the editorial writer in La Presse, Mr. Guy Cormier, did not mince his words and put on kid gloves when he maintained, on June 3 of this year, that this political principle, "divide and rule", set down by one of the Prime Minister's predecessors, namely Mr. Mackenzie King, no longer applied nowadays.

Mr. Speaker, in the twenty fifth parliament of Canada I had the opportunity in my maiden speech of following the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette). This is now the twenty sixth parliament of Canada and, as I watched the spectacle across from me this evening, while it seemed to me my maiden speech was a very important one, the speech I hope to be able to make this evening will be perhaps the most important I shall ever make in this house.
I represent the riding of York North and in it, from north to south, we have the towns of Sutton, Newmarket, Aurora and Richmond Hill. Many of these towns were settled by United Empire Loyalists who left the United States during the rebellion against Britain, to live in a land loyal to British tradition and constitutional monarchy. These people preferred king and country to the so-called war of independence. They settled in Canada, and Canada has become strong with their strength and courage.
When the Loyalists came to Canada they bore with them the flag of union, the union jack, and it flies proudly today throughout my riding. The descendants of these people are still loyal to those traditions even today. In my riding we recall the indomitable little firebrand and rebel, William Lyon Mackenzie, our loyal representatives over the years, Aylesworth, Mulock, King, all leaders in government, pathfinders over the years,

reformers loyal to the traditions of the flag of their day.
Flags, Mr. Speaker, are a strange creation. They are used as merely pieces of silk held aloft in some instances to identify the status of a chief, to mark the arrival of a leader, or to denote the arrival of an enemy.
They were first used in India and China, primarily for the purpose of identification. Other uses arose. They were used to show the forces of the leader. In medieval times, the flag was the first point of attack. When the flag had fallen, consternation among the flagless army ensued, and the battle was soon lost. In victory, the flag rallied the victorious army to the chase to press on to the eventual rout of the enemy. Moreover, at sea the flag was more than a rallying point; it became a method of signalling. All this, of course, is aside from mere decoration and display for which flags have been used. What English seaman has forgotten the white naval ensign of Nelson at the battle of Trafalgar? One of my hon. friends says it was the red ensign. In fact, that ensign is a good example of a flag which served as identification of the status of a commander, as a signal, as a rallying point and later for decoration and display after the battle.
In one word, then, Mr. Speaker, flags have become for us after all these uses, symbols. They become the physical manifestations of the emotions for which they stand. They remind us of our past, indicate our present status and point with pride to the future.
One of the flags I intend to vote for when the final division bells ring is the union jack. It reminds Canadians of their past traditions. It indicates our present status in the commonwealth of nations and points with pride to our future close association with Great Britain. The other flag for which I intend to vote will be a distinctive Canadian flag which will remind us of our Canadian past with a world recognized symbol of that past, the maple leaf; it will show our present status as an independent nation, being, in the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), a flag which is Canada's own and only Canada's. Moreover, it will point with pride to our future as a united nation-one Canada from sea to sea, strong, powerful and free.
I wish to direct my remarks to the amendment which has been proposed by the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), that is, the proposal to submit this question to a national referendum or plebiscite. I am astonished that the Leader of the Opposition

should have made this suggestion because as late as last Wednesday speaking on C.B.C. television, he had this to say:
Put this matter of the flag before the Canadian people and I fear the result.
On the same program, he said: "You say, should it go to the Canadian people? I say, no."
You wouldn't be quoting him out of context, would you?

For someone who is well versed in British traditions as well as in the parliamentary traditions of this country to propose a referendum, is astonishing. A referendum strikes directly at the entire concept of British parliamentary democracy. As the encyclopaedia of Canada says at Volume 5, page 232:
A referendum is a constitutional device whereby a question with which the legislature does not feel itself capable of dealing is referred to the electorate in a popular vote. It has been borrowed from the United States.
The same encyclopaedia concludes:
It is clear, however, that both the referendum and the initiative are alien to the spirit of British parliamentary government.
Why are they alien? The answer can be found in the words of Professor Dicey, the late distinguished expert on constitutional law and practice. Professor Dicey says this:
The referendum diminishes the importance of parliamentary debate and thereby detracts from the influence of parliament. That this must be so admits of no denial; a veto, whether it be exercised by a king or by an electorate, lessens the power of the legislature.
Of course, it is easy for us to see why the referendum has been used so often in the United States. There the division of powers is definite. In the federal government, and in each and every state government, the legislative branch is distinct from the executive branch. The president is separated from congress; a governor is separated from the state legislature. Thus the referendum or plebiscite is resorted to. Incidentally, the Encyclopaedia Canadiana, volume 8 defines plebiscite this way:
A device for ascertaining the opinion of the electorate on a question, but not involving any legal obligation on the legislative body to act upon it.
When the executive branch and the legislative branch in the United States disagreed, resort was made to the people to solve the disagreement and the public at large was asked to vote. The executive arm would request the referendum, the people would vote, 20220-277J

and then the legislature would be forced to act in accord with the simple yes or no of the people. That may be compatible with the separation of powers in the United States. It is not compatible with the British and Canadian parliamentary and ministerial tradition. As the distinguished professor of government, William B. Munro said in his book "American Influences on Canadian Government":
In Canada a provincial legislature is elected, and a ministry is placed in power to carry out the will of the legislature. If, then, the people can directly initiate legislation, if they can directly enact or reject legislation, the whole principle of unified ministerial responsibility is seriously impaired. For a ministry cannot serve two masters -the legislative body insisting on one thing, and the electorate requiring something different.
Our system of government is based upon the direct responsibility of the ministry to the legislature and of the legislature to the people. There is no "double harness" here; a ministry does not ride the legislature and ride the people at one and the same time. The ministry proposes to parliament; parliament acts, and if parliament does not approve, the ministry tenders its resignation and the people vote for a new leadership. It is, I think, significant that in the 1920's-and this will interest hon. gentleman opposite in particular-the Progressive Conservative premier of Ontario, Hon. George Ferguson, announced that there would be no more popular votes on the liquor question in the province but that the legislature and cabinet would deal with the issue and take full responsibility for it-as ought to be done in any scheme of government based on the direct responsibility of the ministry to the legislature, and of the legislature to the people. This government, too, has that responsibility, and if parliament disagrees, the government will resign; or if the people disapprove, they may vote out the government at the next general election. But a parliament is elected to decide all questions of government and take responsibility for its decisions.
One party is given a mandate by the people on the basis of that party's leadership and the platform presented at the time of the election; another party forms an opposition, Her Majesty's loyal opposition, to play its role in that responsibility. A referendum isolates an issue; demands a simple yes or no. At times of great emotion-and any referendum on the question of national symbols would be a time of great emotion-a simple yes or no cannot decide governmental policy. At times such as this we have all been

The balkanization of this country would be a sad sight; the spectacle would become demeaning to parliament, because the legislature would be ignored in this particular process. If we had a referendum or a plebiscite the men elected to this legislature would be left to stand and watch, to abdicate their responsibility. It is little wonder, then, that the referendum has almost never been used in Canada- I think, twice-and I believe never in British political history. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I want to dispel any misunderstanding. I never said that there was an arrangement or an understanding. All I said was, and I think I will be confirmed by all the house leaders, that it would be advisable, the decent thing to do, to allow the other leaders the same range of discussion as the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition in their speeches. One of the parties did not agree and it was for that reason I said a few minutes ago, in order to correct the leader of the Ralliement Cre-ditiste, that if I did not object to his not being limited it was because I thought this was the proper thing to do for the leaders.

I rise on a question of personal privilege, Mr. Speaker. The Minister of Justice has just indicated to the house

that an arrangement had been made. Of course, not all the house leaders agreed to it, and we will go along with that. He has called to our attention that special privileges were to be extended to the party leaders. Since when has he taken it upon himself to deny to every member of this house the same right? We all arrived here by the same method and we are all entitled to the same privileges. The Prime Minister said that there would be freedom of debate for every hon. member in this house, and what the Minister of Justice is suggesting now would deny that right.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The remarks made by the hon. member confirm the suggestion I made just a moment ago that we are getting away from the point which should be decided at this moment as to whether or not a legitimate point of order was raised by the Minister of Justice. I would appreciate any further comments on that specific point.

Mr. Speaker, it would seem to me that the point of order made by the Minister of Justice would have had considerable force if it had been made at the right time. In other words, I would think that when we have an amendment before this house it would make a lot of sense if we were to discuss the amendment. This does not appear to be the rule. 1 further suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that to change the rules in the middle of the debate to extend privileges to certain members that are not available to other members would be a serious mistake.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
If your ruling, Mr. Speaker, is going to follow the argument put forward by the last person who spoke, I would be quite content. However, in case you are still in doubt, I want to support what he just said. You simply cannot change the rules part way through a debate.
Let me say that there is no misunderstanding. The government house leader has mentioned an attempted arrangement amongst the house leaders, and I think in doing so he has gone beyond what he should do. Why does he mention in the house that there was a meeting of house leaders and one did not agree? Well, all right, I did not agree. Let us be frank about the thing. I did not agree because you cannot impose this type of closure on members of this house. May I direct your attention to the rule of relevancy and the comments on relevancy on page 111 of Beau-chesne's fourth edition:

Relevancy is not easy to define. A wrong comprehension of it may have a serious effect on the freedom of speech. Members are often deprived of their right to speak on the pretext that their remarks are irrelevant when as a matter of fact they refer to matters perhaps remote but yet related, even indirectly, to the question under debate. In borderline cases the member should be given the benefit of the doubt. A great deal of latitude must be allowed in the House of Commons which is a forum where every phase of public affairs can be discussed and every member has the right to be heard, even if in doing so he sometimes disregards the rigidity of procedure.
Finally, may I say that yesterday Mr. Speaker dealt with the subject of relevancy as recorded on page 4307 of Hansard. You can read there where he said it was difficult to-
Read it all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

The Prime Minister was mixing up the two resolutions, (a) and (b) and a point was raised. Then, Mr. Speaker said this:
The point before the house is a flag for Canada. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your decision and would like to say that not only have we a split resolution but I have a split speech. About a half an hour ago, when the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) tried to delay me, I was attempting to indicate what I felt about the resolution and the amendment. I was pointing out the reasons surrounding the introduction of this resolution into the house, and the great desire on the part of the government to ask parliament all of a sudden to confirm a new flag design.
I might refer back to not very long ago, to the day when the Prime Minister came into the house and outlined the priorities in legislation which he considered were necessary for the house to consider before we could recess.
At that time the flag resolution was not even considered a priority piece of legislation. All of a sudden, for some reason best known to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), parliament is confronted with this emotional debate at a time when many, if not most, of the promises made by the government during the election campaign of April, 1963 remain unfulfilled. I say: why this great haste all of a sudden? Why this argument that the government must implement a particular promise within the time limit indicated when it was in opposition, because it was a solemn commitment which must be undertaken? When was this solemn commitment given, and where, and how often during the election campaigns of 1962 and 1963? I should like to refer to an interview which the Prime Minister, when leader of the opposition, gave in my constituency at Amherst, Nova Scotia. A number of questions were asked him by a

Canadian Flag
reporter regarding the flag matter. Among the questions put to him at that time was the following:
Do you think Quebec will oppose anything except a flag with the fleur-de-lis in it? Must they have this part in it?
The Prime Minister's reply was:
Well, we would have our Quebec ministers in our cabinet decide what the design would be and they would make their views very clear at that time, I am sure.
In the same interview, the right hon. gentleman stated that he would not be mentioning the flag, or this new proposed flag, when he spoke in Amherst that evening. Well, I am afraid statements of this kind could be forthcoming from many areas of Canada. Indeed, my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) pointed out last night that the British Columbia section of the Liberal party, when putting out its program, omitted any reference to a new flag because of the known feeling about a new flag design in that province. To say that we are today discussing the flag issue because it was a commitment made to the electors in 1963 is in my opinion the height of ridiculousness-nothing could be farther from the truth.
I think the emergency committee to save the Canadian red ensign which signed an open letter to the Prime Minister sets this point out very well when it states:
It is said that our representatives were elected to decide the flag. There was more than one plank in the Liberal platform, and many who voted for your party's flag resolution, sir, did not dream that a "distinctive flag" must exclude all symbols of our heritage. Surely, most Canadians rejected a flag change when the majority rejected the party that proposed it. The reference in the platform to a "distinctive" flag was misleading. A flag "distinctive" from what? The adjective is irrelevant to the debate. It is the right slogan for the wrong battle-a battle won years ago when Canadians rightly demanded a flag distinct from the great union flag of Britain. The resulting "distinctive" flag was, of course, the Canadian fed ensign, which was so described in the order in council of 1945. The ensign, bearing the shield of Canada, cannot be confused with any other flag on earth. We are disturbed by the cranked-up campaign to exchange this distinctive flag, rich in meaning, for one created out of whole cloth which many millions of us think distinctly undistinguished.
Surely a government sincerely concerned for national unity would honour and perpetuate the graphic symbols of both French and British founding peoples. The present government, apparently unable to reconcile the legitimate claims of each, is ducking the problem by erasing the memory of both. Three quarters of the United States flag is devoted to reminding Americans that they began as 13 British colonies. Unlike Dahomey, Gabon, Mali, and the Malagasy republic, Canada was not born yesterday. We neither need nor want a

brand new flag. Should you doubt this, sir, we urge you to put it to the test. Only a plebiscite will relieve the building bitterness of a victimized majority.
Canadians know that a parliament, precariously balanced, should not decide this issue. They know that members are not being asked to vote for a flag, but against an election. They know that a plebiscite will clear the air and unite all who honour the democratic process. They know that this issue, unlike most others, requires no arcane knowledge and no deep study. It is an issue on which every Canadian has an opinion, and should have a vote.
What do Canadians have to say? I should like to quote from some editorials in various newspapers across this country which feel that a plebiscite is the only fair way in which to handle this question at the present time. Before I do so, I should like to say this: It can never be said that the Prime Minister did not have every possible opportunity to keep this matter out of politics, to keep it from becoming a partisan political debate. He was given the opportunity. Indeed, he appeared to have taken the opportunity, and then, for some reason best known to himself, he backed down. He half committed himself to a plebiscite in this house by giving each and every member the right to vote in favour of the red ensign, or of this new maple leaf design which he considers to be a distinctive flag. The Prime Minister need only have selected one of his members, allowed him to introduce the resolution, and said to the country: There will be no vote of confidence on this matter; it is a matter which each member of parliament can decide freely and on the basis of his knowledge, both personal and with regard to his constituency. If this had been done there would be no one in this country today asking for a national plebiscite. The people would feel that their representatives would be responsible enough to make the fairest possible decision.
But what has happened? The whip has been cracked; the people of this country have been told it is a flag which the Prime Minister has indicated is his personal choice-and let there be no mistake about that. Mr. Val Sears in a column in the Toronto Star on May 20 last, pointed this out clearly and concisely when he said:
As drinks were served and the newspapermen nibbled on sandwiches, Mr. Pearson brought out several flag designs on cardboard, selected one with a cluster of three maple leaves and two blue bands and placed it on the mantelpiece as his choice.
He said he was prepared to have the government stand or fall on the maple leaf flag.

The Prime Minister was careful, however, to make clear that the flag on the mantel was his personal choice.
Well, Mr. Speaker, it is going to be everybody's personal choice, apparently, unless Canadians are given some opportunity to indicate what their personal choice might be; because we are told that we either vote for it or the public will not only have a plebiscite as to the maple leaf design but they will have a plebiscite as to the government of this country. And even at this late date, if the Prime Minister had any wisdom left I would say he would not want to let the Canadian people make that decision at this time.
Hear, hear.

What do the newspapers of this country say? Apparently the Prime Minister is becoming more selective as to newspapers and newspapermen than he was when he was leader of the opposition, because I understood only eight reporters were invited to this little get-together. These were eight very carefully selected gentlemen. I know most of them, and they are very nice gentlemen; but I understand there are 120 such gentlemen in the press gallery and I would think they would be somewhat offended at not having been invited.
And a young lady.

Yes; not only one young lady, but a very attractive young lady. If the Prime Minister had been wise he would have invited her. Certainly had I been the prime minister I would have seen that the young lady was there too. However, seeing that the Prime Minister is selective in the reporters he chooses, he might also be as selective in the newspapers he now reads. With this thought in mind, Mr. Speaker, I would like to put the views of a few of the newspaper editors in this country on the record so the Prime Minister may take a look at what they suggest and how they view this autocratic attitude he has with regard to his personal pennant. The daily Gleaner of May 27, 1964, had this to say:
The only logical way the Pearson government could get out of the flag impasse in which it now finds itself would be to submit the red ensign and the maple leaf designs to a national referendum, with the winner automatically becoming Canada's flag.
We go to the other end of the country, where the Vancouver Province says this about Mr. Pearson. The heading to the article
Canadian Flag
is "Mr. Pearson flirts with political suicide". The concluding part of the article is as follows:
Mr. Pearson's Liberal predecessors, Mackenzie King and Louis St. Laurent, understood the political danger of trying to invent a new Canadian flag. They knew that such a move would do more harm than good to national unity and they steered well away from the flag controversy.
Now Mr. Pearson has headed directly into the hurricane zone.
The winner of the Nobel peace prize has become a contender for another distinction-that of kindling the worst racial conflict in our country's history.
There is not much talk about national unity in that editorial, Mr. Speaker. And for my good friend from Bonavista-Twillingate I will quote from the daily News of St. John's, Newfoundland, which had this to say:
In fact, it might be imagined that it would be better in the first instance to sound popular opinion by means of a referendum. And only if it should be shown by this means that there is an overwhelming demand for a new emblem, should any change be considered.
Take note, Mr. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill).
He isn't here.

The Charlottetown Guardian had this to say:
There are a lot of people in Canada who may want to retain the old flag but do not want yet another national election at this time. This issue would present them with a painful choice. It could be averted by a national referendum, thus leaving the country at large to make a free choice in the matter. But Mr. Pearson will have none of that.
I now come to the Toronto Telegram. I might mention that while this paper has been a strong supporter of the Conservative party, I remember that not very long ago it was a strong supporter of the Liberal party. It had this to say in an editorial entitled "Statesmanship":
It is highly probable that the Progressive Conservative opposition will move an amendment to Pearson s flag legislation asking for such a plebiscite. Mr. Andrew Brewin, the N.D.P. member from Toronto-Greenwood, has expressed the belief that most of his colleagues would vote for it Mr. Arnold Peters, N.D.P. member from Timiska-mmg, and New Democrat Barry Mather of B C have reinforced this assumption.
I wonder if they have talked to their leader on this matter and convinced him that he also should be supporting this amendment. Another issue of the Toronto Telegram had this to say:	.
In the Telegram's view the Prime Minister has been recklessly unwise in rejecting the proposal for

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion a plebiscite on the issue. Only by such a device can the people of the nation freely and clearly express their choice.
The Victoria daily Colonist had this to say: Parliament has yet to express itself on the flag resolution but even among the doubts expressed by M-P.'s of all groups about the new design, and preference by many for a national plebiscite, the trend indicates that the government s measure will pass...
Unless at the last minute M.P.'s vote on the new flag as conscience and personal choice dictate it will never be known whether their decision is based on conviction or political expediency. And this will acerbate the division of public opinion that exists on the subject of a national flag.
Then the Quebec Chronicle had this to say: First things first is a good rule even for prime ministers. The flag issue now before parliament is unlikely to be over in a few days; it is bound to generate a great deal of bitterness in the country, even though the intentions of the government are above reproach.
For one thing, the country must know why Mr. Pearson had to move in such a hurry. Is he trying to do with the flag what Judy LaMarsh coudn't do with her pension plan? Or does he consider a national flag such a trivial piece of business that it wasn't really worth while consulting anybody on its design?
Mr. Speaker, those are some of the questions that some of the newspapers in this country are asking the Prime Minister about a national referendum.
May I call it ten o'clock.

(Subject matter of questions debated under adjournment motion).
A motion to adjourn the house under provisional standing order 39A deemed to have been moved:

Mr. Speaker, on June 10 I asked a question of the Associate Minister of National Defence in the following terms:

Is the minister aware that a civilian cook named Lome Edward Pace, with 12 years of good service in the R.C.N. and two years as a civilian cook with the H.C.A.F. in Halifax, has been discharged for taking home a 50 cent cake? Would the minister investigate the matter-
Mr. Speaker at that time ruled that the matter should be on the order paper, and I indicated according to the procedure relevant that I should like to discuss it in this period after ten o'clock.
Despite the fact that the question was ruled as one for the order paper, the associate minister of defence promptly conducted an investigation into the matter, and as a consequence of his investigation I received the following letter from him dated June 11:
Dear Mr. Regan:
I wish to inform you that I have had the dismissal of Mr. Lome Edward Pace, cook at the combined mess, R.C.A.F. Gorsebrook, Halifax, investigated.
I am satisfied that the action taken was unduly harsh, and I have directed that Mr. Pace be reinstated forthwith.
From the time of his release to the date of his reinstatement, he will be considered as under suspension without pay.
Yours very truly, Lucien Cardin
I should like to use these few moments to thank the associate minister of defence for his prompt action in this matter. Too often in years gone by it has been the way of ministers of the crown to tend to defend actions of their subordinates which have been too extreme. I think it is very much to the credit of our present associate minister of defence that he took this prompt action to rectify this injustice.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that this case has ended happily. It was one in which a man was discharged by his superiors for taking home a cake which was more than a day old. Early information indicated that this cake would have ended up in the garbage; I now understand this is not the case but that it would have been used for pudding. Someone said to me a few moments ago that the proof of the pudding is in the eating. I think that while this case has ended very well we must wonder how many Lome Edward Paces there are whose cases do not come to the attention of parliament or to ministers of the crown.
In this instance radio station CHNS in Halifax and Edmund Morris, a former member of this house, brought the matter to public attention. After that I contacted the minister during the question period, and I

understand the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) had also contacted him in this regard. Certainly he should have some share in the credit for bringing the matter to the attention of the authorities. However, the case spells out, I think, the need for haste in providing an independent arbitration board to deal not only with discharge grievances but grievances of civil servants and government employees, including the hourly paid classifications. I have in mind grievances arising not only from discharge but from working conditions, classification and other matters.
As we all know, at the present time there is a committee investigating a system of collective bargaining for civil servants and other government employees, and presumably this
